rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh says wāw and yā remain unchanged when the final radical is itself wāw or yā: weakening would add heaviness, ambiguity, or excessive loss instead of ease.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن الواو والياء لا تعلان واللام ياء أو واو لأنهم إذا فعلوا ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These forms otherwise follow the patterns of qāla yaqūlu, bāʿa yabīʿu, khāfa yakhāfu, and hāba yahābu.
rows.anchor: فهذه الحروف تجري مجرى قال يقول وباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the middle radical is hamza, the hamza at the end creates two hamzas in one word, so the second cannot be softened between hamza and its neighboring sound.
rows.anchor: تكن لتجعل اللام بين بين من قبل أنهما في كلمة واحدة وأنهما لا يفترقان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the two hamzas become especially heavy, speakers turn the final lām into yā and remove its resemblance to hamza.
rows.anchor: ازدادتا ثقلا فحولوا اللام وأخرجوها من شبه الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʿil forms follow jāʾa, not khaṭāyā, since their hamza is present outside the plural rather than appearing only in the plural.
rows.anchor: فاعل بمنزلة جاء ولم يجعلوا هذا بمنزلة خطايا لأن الهمز لم يعرض في الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khaṭāyā follows maṭāyā because its hamza arises in the plural.
rows.anchor: وأما خطايا فحيث كانت همزتها تعرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In faʿāʾil, the yā is always hamzated; Sībawayh compares this to faʿāʿil.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن ياء فعائل أبدا مهموزة لا تكون إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fawāʿil plural of jiʾtu is jawāʾ, like shuwāʾ from shāwtu, and keeps the singular pattern in the plural.
rows.anchor: تقول من شأوت شواء فتجزيها في الجمع على حد ما كانت عليه في الواحد لأنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿāʾil from jiʾtu and suʾtu follows the khaṭāyā pattern, yielding jiyāyā and suwāyā.
rows.anchor: وأما فعائل من جئت وسؤت فكخطايا تقول

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl analyzes the final radical in jāʾa, shāʾa, and similar forms as inverted.
rows.anchor: وأما الخليل ms865 فكان يزعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ajjāj uses lāth in a line where the expected form has hamza, evidence for avoiding a single hamza.
rows.anchor: إذ كانوا يقلبون كراهية الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭarīf b. Tamīm uses shāk in his line, another poetic form that avoids hamza.
rows.anchor: وقال لطريف بن تميم العنبري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most Arabs say lāth and shāk silāḥahu; Sībawayh distinguishes those who delete hamza from those whose forms seem not to invert the final radical.
rows.anchor: يقول لاث وشاك سلاحه فهؤلاء حذفوا الهمزة وهؤلاء كأنهم لم يقلبوا اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because deletion would put a silent alif next to a silent yā, this supports the view that jāʾ's hamza substitutes for the middle radical.
rows.anchor: التي تبدل من العين وكلا القولين حسن جميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh accepts both analyses of jāʾa as sound.
rows.anchor: التي تبدل من العين وكلا القولين حسن جميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿāʾil from jiʾtu and suʾtu yields jiyāʾ and suwāʾ because the hamza is not newly introduced in the plural.
rows.anchor: لأنها ليست همزة تعرض في جمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In faʿlal forms from jiʾtu and qaraʾtu, the hamzas remain together; there is no inversion because the root has no underlying wāw or yā.
rows.anchor: وأما فعلل من جئت وقرأت فإنك تقول فيه جيأي وقرأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the hamza is already part of the singular, its plural remains fixed, as in qarāʾ and jiyāʾ.
rows.anchor: فإذا جمعت قلت قراء وجياء لأن الهمزة ثابتة في الواحد وليست تعرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿāʿil from jiʾtu and suʾtu yields jiyāyā and suwāyā; a hamzated final radical blocks the yā-inversion found in jāʾ and khaṭāyā.
rows.anchor: لم يكن من قلب اللام ياء بد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the inversion analysis, the corresponding forms should be jiyāʾ and shiwāʾ, since the original hamza stays in the singular and only a wāw or yā is shifted to the end in fāʿil.
rows.anchor: لأنهما همزتا الأصل التي تكون في الواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms derived from ṣadiʾa turn the final hamza into yā in ifʿallala and related patterns; this follows the Khalīlian analysis.
rows.anchor: وأما افعللت من صدئت فاصدأيت تقلبها ياء كما تقلبها في مفعلل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fiyāʿil from suʾtu and jiʾtu follows faʿāʿil, with plural-only hamza producing siyāyā and jiyāyā.
rows.anchor: تقول جيايا وسيايا لأنها همزة عرضت في الجمع

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl parses suʾtuhu suʾāʾiyya on faʿāliyya, like ʿalāniyya.
rows.anchor: فقال هي فعالية بمنزلة علانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who say suwāya delete the hamza, as in hār and lāth; most speakers also leave the hamza out of malak, whose original form contains it.
rows.anchor: كما اجتمع أكثرهم على ترك الهمز في ملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites an unnamed poet's malʾak for malak and says maʾlaka and malʾaka mean risāla, 'message.'
rows.anchor: تنزل من جو السماء يصوب

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl treats masāʾīhi, ashyāʾ, and ashāwī as inverted forms; qusī is a parallel inversion from quwūs.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن مسائيه فقال هي مقلوبة وكذلك أشياء وأشاوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's al-yawmi al-yami is an inverted form of al-yawm.
rows.anchor: مروان مروان أخو اليوم اليمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inversion avoids the heaviness of adjacent waw and hamza, which are both difficult sounds.
rows.anchor: فمسائية إنما كان حدها مساوئة فكرهوا الواو مع الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashyāʾ is traced to shayʾā; ashāwī is traced to ashāyā, with hamza moved before shīn and yā changed to wāw.
rows.anchor: أصل أشياء شيئاء فكرهوا منها مع الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inversion in items such as ṭaʾmana/iṭmaʾanna is limited to forms whose meaning matches another form after inversion; it is not productive.
rows.anchor: فإنما حمل هذه الأشياء على القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jadhab and jabadh are independent roots rather than inversions because each pattern is productive across meanings and conjugations.
rows.anchor: لأن ذلك يطرد فيهما في كل معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl treats kalā and kull as two separate forms, not an inversion or a form containing a recognizable affix.
rows.anchor: وأما كلا وكل فمن لفظين لأنه ليس ههنا قلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some verbs can take two direct objects, though a speaker may stop after the first or continue with a second object.
rows.anchor: الذي يتعداه فعله إلى مفعولين فإن شئت اقتصرت على المفعول الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Choosing someone from a group can take two direct objects after the preposition is omitted; Sībawayh cites Qur'an 7:155 as an example.
rows.anchor: واختار موسى قومه سبعين رجلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming and giving a kunya can take two objects; daʿawtuhu takes two only when it means naming, while calling someone to an action takes one.
rows.anchor: ودعوته زيدا إذا أردت دعوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many such verbs originally govern a phrase introduced by a preposition; when the preposition is omitted, the verb governs the complement directly.
rows.anchor: أفعال توصل بحروف الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's astaghfiru Allāha dhanban represents astaghfiru Allāha min dhanbin, with min omitted.
rows.anchor: أستغفر الله ذنبا لست محصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib's amartuka al-khayr means amartuka bi-l-khayr, with bāʾ omitted.
rows.anchor: أمرتك الخير فافعل ما أمرت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mutalammis's ālaytu ḥubb al-ʿIrāq means ālaytu ʿalā ḥubb al-ʿIrāq, with ʿalā omitted.
rows.anchor: آليت حب العراق الدهر أطعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nubbiʾtu Zaydan means 'I was told about Zayd'; ʿan and ʿalā do not omit like bāʾ, nor does min in a positive clause.
rows.anchor: وكما تقول نبئت زيدا يقول ذاك أي عن زيد وليست عن وعلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Astaghfiru Allāha dhanban and amartuka al-khayr are uncommon constructions used only by some speakers.
rows.anchor: بعضهم فأما سميت وكنيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With sammaytu and kannaytu, bāʾ works as in ʿaraftuhu bi-Zaydin; the prepositional construction differs in meaning from the direct-object construction.
rows.anchor: فأما سميت وكنيت فإنما دخلتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq's ikhtīra al-rijāla shows the direct-object construction with ikhtāra.
rows.anchor: منا الذي اختير الرجال سماحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq also uses nubbiʾtu ʿAbda Allāhi bi-l-jawwi as an example of a verb taking its complement through bāʾ.
rows.anchor: نبئت عبد الله بالجو أصبحت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This treatment is limited: verbs do not all permit preposition deletion, and verbs do not all take one or two objects.
rows.anchor: كما أنه ليس كل فعل يتعدى الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ailments commonly use faʿila yafʿalu, with a verbal noun on faʿal and an adjective on faʿil; Sībawayh illustrates the pattern with ḥabiṭa and ḥabija.
rows.anchor: وذلك حبط يحبط حبطا وهو حبط وحبج يحبج حبجا وهو حبج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective may instead be faʿīl, as in mariḍa yamraḍu and marīḍ.
rows.anchor: نحو مرض يمرض مرضا وهو مريض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqima may be said with kasra or by some Arabs with fatḥa, compared with karuma and karīm.
rows.anchor: وقالوا سقم يسقم سقما وهو سقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqm and ḥuzn are verbal nouns; ḥuzn is grouped with disease because it is an affliction.
rows.anchor: جعلوه بمنزلة المرض لأنه داء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wajila and similar states of fear follow the same verb and noun pattern because they are close in meaning to wajiʿa.
rows.anchor: وقرب المعنى وجل يوجل وجلا وهو وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blindness of the heart is treated as an affliction that strikes the heart.
rows.anchor: إنما جعله بلاء أصاب قلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear and terror verbs such as faziʿa, fariqa, wajila, and wajira use this pattern because fear reaches the heart as illness reaches the body.
rows.anchor: لأنه داء قد وصل إلى فؤاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awjara joins the faʿila pattern in a related sense; faʿila and afʿala can coexist, as in other paired adjective patterns.
rows.anchor: فأدخلوا أفعل ههنا على فعل لأن فعلا وأفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farriqtuhu and fazzaʿtuhu mean farriqtu minhu and faziʿtu minhu; the preposition min has been omitted.
rows.anchor: كما قالوا أمرتك الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khashiyahu, khashyatan, and khāsh follow a derivational pattern like raḥima and rāḥim, even though the surface forms differ.
rows.anchor: وقالوا خشيته خشية وهو خاش كما قالوا رحم وهو راحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opposite states such as arisha, batira, fariḥa, and jaḏila use the same verb, noun, and adjective pattern.
rows.anchor: أشر يأشر أشرا وهو أشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms such as jaḏlān, kaslān, and sakrān pair with jaḏil, kasil, and sakir, showing related faʿlān and faʿil formations.
rows.anchor: وقالوا جذلان كما قالوا كسلان وكسل وسكران وسكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nashiṭa has the adjective nashīṭ, while nashāṭ parallels suqām; saqīm and suqām are compared with jamīl and jamāl.
rows.anchor: وقالوا نشط ينشط وهو نشيط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defects such as sahk and qinam are treated like diseases, with corresponding nouns sahka and qinma.
rows.anchor: وقالوا سهك يسهك سهكا وهو سهك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAqara and ʿāqir follow the same pattern as saqima and sāqim, and māthik provides a parallel adjective.
rows.anchor: وقالوا عقرت عقرا كما قالوا سقمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khamaṭ is contrasted with qinam, which Sībawayh glosses as sahk.
rows.anchor: وقالوا خمط خمطا وهو خمط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arija describes wind movement and brightness, while ḥamisa describes agitation and anger; these share a semantic group of arousal.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولهم أرج يأرج أرجا وهو أرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥmasa occurs alongside ḥamisa; in this group afʿal functions like faʿlān, as in ghaḍbān.
rows.anchor: وصار أفعل ههنا بمنزلة فعلان وغضبان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afʿal can also join faʿlān forms and generally keeps the same verb and verbal-noun pattern.
rows.anchor: فلا يفارقهما في بناء الفعل والمصدر كثيرا

rows.speaker: أبو الخطاب
rows.claim: Abū al-Khaṭṭāb reports that ahyam and haymān both mean thirsty.
rows.anchor: رجل أهيم وهيمان يريدون شيئا واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salis, qaliq, naziq, and ghaliq are grouped with agitation because they denote lightness and movement.
rows.anchor: قلق يقلق قلقا وهو قلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghaliq can describe nonhuman things too, since they have become light or loose in their place.
rows.anchor: وكذلك الغلق في غير الأناسي لأنه قد خف من مكانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unpleasant qualities such as ʿasr, shakās, laqas, and laḥaz follow faʿila yafʿalu with faʿil adjectives because their meanings resemble ailments.
rows.anchor: لتقاربها في المعنى وذلك ما تعذر عليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqima and ʿasura can both yield faʿīl adjectives; nakida has both nakid and an-kad, and laḥija is close in meaning to ʿasura.
rows.anchor: وقد قالوا عسر الأمر وهو عسير كما قالوا سقم وهو سقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laḥija is included in the same group because its meaning is close to ʿusr.
rows.anchor: لأن معناه قريب من معنى العسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A phrase used as a name may be preserved exactly as it was in ordinary speech; examples include taʾabbaṭa sharran and barq naḥruhu.
rows.anchor: وذلك قول العرب في رجل يسمى تأبط شرا هذا تأبط شرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A line attributed to a poet from Banū Ṭahiyya leaves dharā ḥubban intact, illustrating a phrase used as a name.
rows.anchor: كأنه جبهة ذرى حبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Changing a quoted phrase when it becomes a name would produce forms people do not use, such as turning a verse into an altered name.
rows.anchor: فمن قال أغير هذا دخل عليه أن يسمى الرجل ببيت شعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's line beginning kadhabtum wa-bayti Allāh is another example of a phrase preserved as a name.
rows.anchor: بني شاب قرناها تصر وتحلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet's phrase aḥaqq al-khayli bi-l-rakḍ al-muʿār is cited as another unchanged quotation.
rows.anchor: فكذلك هذه الضروب إذا كانت أسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quoted names are not dualized or pluralized internally; an outer kull or kilā may be added while the quoted phrase stays unchanged.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الاسم إذا كان محكيا لم يثن ولم يجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quoted names are not annexed or diminished; a shortened form may be made by deleting part and treating the remainder like an annexed form.
rows.anchor: ولا تضيفه إلى شيء إلا أن تقول هذا تأبط شرا صاحبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Multiword names such as khayrun minka, maʾkhūdhun bika, and ḍāriban rajulan retain their ordinary phrase form.
rows.anchor: وسألت الخليل عن رجل يسمي خيرا منك أو مأخوذا بك

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says a woman named khayrun minka or ḍāriban rajulan keeps tanwīn because the phrase is not complete at khayr or ḍārib.
rows.anchor: ليس منتهى الاسم ولا مأخوذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Phrases such as lā khayran minhu laka and lā ḍāriban rajulan laka show that tanwīn remains in these quoted constructions.
rows.anchor: قولهم لا خيرا منه لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names formed from two separate words such as ʿāqilatun labībatun and ʿāqilun labībun keep each word's ordinary inflection and tanwīn.
rows.anchor: بعاقلة لبيبة أو عاقل لبيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a single feminine name ʿĀqila, quoting the indefinite form may be allowed, but the preferred form drops tanwīn; the two-word phrase is best treated as a quotation.
rows.anchor: الوجه ترك الصرف والوجه في ذلك الأول

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl treats min Zayd and ʿan Zayd as changed compound names, not ordinary case-governed phrases, because these prepositions depend on a complement.
rows.anchor: وسألت الخليل عن رجل يسمى من زيد وعن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A compound like wazn sabʿa or khamsata ʿashar is treated as a compound proper name, not as a preserved utterance.
rows.anchor: قلت هذا وزن سبعة فتجعله بمنزلة طلحة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl treats fī Zayd as a heavy compound name; its final yā can be mobile in the accusative, unlike the separate min and ʿan compounds.
rows.anchor: فأقول هذا في زيد كما ثقلته

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Inna-ma, anna-ma, kaʾanna-ma, ḥaythu-ma, and imma remain quoted forms because mā is not fused into a single word as in ḥaḍramawt.
rows.anchor: هن حكايات لأن ما هذه لم تجعل

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: The mā in ḥaythu-ma does not remove the dialectal forms of ḥayth; it instead blocks an from the subjunctive and makes ḥayth conditional.
rows.anchor: ولتدخل حيث في الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's in jazʿan wa-in ijmāl ṣabr is cited to show that the form represents imma.
rows.anchor: فإن جزعا وإن إجمال صبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh says exception illā is like duflā; in 7:20 the form is the exception particle.
rows.anchor: إلا التي للاستثناء بمنزلة دفلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Illā and immā in conditional constructions are treated as quotations.
rows.anchor: وأما إلا وإما في الجزاء فحكاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amma in ammā Zaydun fa-munṭaliq is not quoted and is like shurwā.
rows.anchor: وأما التي في قولك أما زيد فمنطلق فلا تكون حكاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogative ammā and allā are quoted forms.
rows.anchor: أما التي في الاستفهام حكاية وألا التي في الاستفهام حكاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allā innahu ẓarīf and ammā innahu ẓarīf behave like qafā and raḥā; laʿalla and forms with added kāf or tā remain quoted.
rows.anchor: اللام هاهنا زائدة بمنزلتها في لأفعلن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hādhā and hāʾulāʾi keep their ordinary form as names because retaining the hāʾ of attention preserves the quoted expression.
rows.anchor: تركته على حاله لأني إذا تركت هاء التنبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh reports hallum as quoted in both dialects; the Tāmīmī hallumman form supports that analysis.
rows.anchor: كأنها لم أدخلت عليها الهاء كما أدخلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lawma, lawla, and the heard phrase lā min ayna are preserved as quotations rather than converted into ordinary names.
rows.anchor: وكذلك لوما ولولا وسمعت من العرب من يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names such as bū Zayd and wa-Zaydan follow their phrase form because these particles occur only as dependents.
rows.anchor: ولو سميت رجلا بو زيد أو وزيدا أو وزيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zayd al-ṭawīl as a name remains a quotation; if al-ṭawīl is made a true adjective, it inflects, and vocative form changes according to whether the whole phrase is called.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد الطويل حكاية بمنزلة زيد منطلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A relative phrase such as al-ladhī raʾaytu stays unchanged because the relative clause completes one name.
rows.anchor: لأن الذي ليس منتهى الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase al-rajul munṭaliqun can be called because it consists of two complete words.
rows.anchor: جاز أن تناديه فتقول يا الرجل منطلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative name cannot take yā ayyuha because it is a single proper name, like al-Naḍr.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن تقول يا أيها الذي رأيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Long coordinated names can revert to ordinary case marking in the vocative; the first item is tanwīnated when it is not the endpoint of the full name.
rows.anchor: قلت يا زيدا وعمرا لأن الاسم قد طال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the first part is a feminine proper name such as Ṭalḥa or Ḥamza, its vocative has no tanwīn, while Zaydan and ʿAmran take it.
rows.anchor: نصبت بغير تنوين كنصب زيد وعمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kā-Zayd and bi-Zayd are quotations because separating kāf or bāʾ would change their form.
rows.anchor: وأما كزيد وبزيد فحكايات لأنك لو أفردت الباء والكاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name ʿAm can preserve its interrogative form; if the speaker instead makes it an independent noun, the phrase becomes ʿan māʾ and is lengthened.
rows.anchor: وإن سميت رجلا عم فأردت أن تحكي في الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When ʿan māʾ is turned into an independent name, it is lengthened and treated as a compound, like the naming construction ʿan Zayd.
rows.anchor: لأنك تريد أن تجعله اسما مفردا
